source_refs.note: Book p. 69-71: derivation of Cramer's rule, results (iii)-(v), Example 13

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book numbers this system "...(ii)" and gives the same number "...(ii)" to the matrix equation \(AX = B\) below. The system should be numbered (i); the matrix equation is (ii).

These are three linear equations in three variables \(x_1, x_2, x_3\) with coefficients and constant terms in the real field \(\mathbb{R}\). We write the above system of equations in matrix form as:
\[AX = B \quad \text{...(ii)}\]
where
\[A = [a_{ij}]_{3\times 3},\ X = \begin{bmatrix}x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3\end{bmatrix}\]
\[B = \begin{bmatrix}b_1 \\ b_2 \\ b_3\end{bmatrix}\]
We know that the matrix equation (2) can be written as: \(X = A^{-1}B\) (if \(A^{-1}\) exists)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book writes "matrix equation (2)"; it means the matrix equation \(AX = B\) numbered (ii).

We have already proved that \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\operatorname{adj} A\) and
\[\operatorname{adj} A = [A'_{ij}]_{3\times 3}\]
\[= \begin{bmatrix}A_{11} & A_{21} & A_{31} \\ A_{12} & A_{22} & A_{32} \\ A_{13} & A_{23} & A_{33}\end{bmatrix}\]
\[(\because A'_{ij} = A_{ji})\]
Thus
\[\begin{bmatrix}x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3\end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{|A|}\begin{bmatrix}A_{11} & A_{21} & A_{31} \\ A_{12} & A_{22} & A_{32} \\ A_{13} & A_{23} & A_{33}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}b_1 \\ b_2 \\ b_3\end{bmatrix}\]
\[= \frac{1}{|A|}\begin{bmatrix}A_{11}b_1 + A_{21}b_2 + A_{31}b_3 \\ A_{12}b_1 + A_{22}b_2 + A_{32}b_3 \\ A_{13}b_1 + A_{23}b_2 + A_{33}b_3\end{bmatrix}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is \(b_1A_{11} + b_2A_{21} + b_3A_{31}\) the determinant in (iii)? \(A_{11}, A_{21}, A_{31}\) are the cofactors of the first column of \(A\), and they do not depend on the first column itself (that column is deleted when a minor is formed). Expanding a determinant along its first column gives "entry times cofactor, added". So if we put \(b_1, b_2, b_3\) in the first column, the expansion is exactly \(b_1A_{11} + b_2A_{21} + b_3A_{31}\).
The rule in words: \(x_k\) = (determinant of \(A\) with column \(k\) replaced by the constants) divided by \(|A|\). Writing \(D = |A|\) and \(D_1, D_2, D_3\) for these determinants: \(x_1 = \frac{D_1}{D}\), \(x_2 = \frac{D_2}{D}\), \(x_3 = \frac{D_3}{D}\). It needs \(D \ne 0\).
The method of solving the system with the help of results (iii), (iv) and (v) is often referred to as Cramer's Rule.

blocks.title: Example 13
blocks.problem:
Use Cramer's rule to solve the system.
\[3x_1 + x_2 - x_3 = -4\]
\[x_1 + x_2 - 2x_3 = -4\]
\[-x_1 + 2x_2 - x_3 = 1\]
steps:
Given: the system above, \(AX = B\) with
\[A = \begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\]
\[B = \begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\]
To find: \(x_1, x_2, x_3\).
Method: Cramer's rule, \(x_k = \frac{D_k}{|A|}\), where \(D_k\) is \(|A|\) with column \(k\) replaced by \(B\). First check \(|A| \ne 0\).

Step 1: Find \(|A|\) (expand along \(R_1\))
\[|A| = \begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 & -1\end{vmatrix}\]
\[= 3(-1+4) - 1\cdot(-1-2)\]
\[\quad - 1\cdot(2+1)\]
\[= 9 + 3 - 3 = 9\]
Why: \(|A| = 9 \ne 0\), so the system has a unique solution and Cramer's rule applies.

Step 2: \(x_1\): replace column 1 by \(B\)
\[x_1 = \frac{1}{9}\begin{vmatrix}-4 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 & -1\end{vmatrix}\]
\[= \frac{-4(-1+4) - 1(4+2) - 1(-8-1)}{9}\]
\[= \frac{-12 - 6 + 9}{9} = \frac{-9}{9} = -1\]
Why: the first column holds the coefficients of \(x_1\); replacing it by the constants gives the numerator of (iii).

Step 3: \(x_2\): replace column 2 by \(B\)
\[x_2 = \frac{1}{9}\begin{vmatrix}3 & -4 & -1 \\ 1 & -4 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{vmatrix}\]
\[= \frac{3(4+2) + 4(-1-2) - 1(1-4)}{9}\]
\[= \frac{18 - 12 + 3}{9} = \frac{9}{9} = 1\]
Why: this is result (iv). The middle term is \(-(-4)(\ldots) = +4(\ldots)\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Cramer's rule: \(x_k = \frac{D_k}{|A|}\), where \(D_k\) is \(|A|\) with column \(k\) replaced by the constants.
2. It works only when \(|A| \ne 0\) (then the solution is unique).
3. It comes from \(X = A^{-1}B = \frac{1}{|A|}(\operatorname{adj} A)B\).
4. Always check the answer in the original equations.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Replacing a row instead of a column by the constants.
2. Replacing the wrong column: for \(x_2\) it is the second column.
3. Sign slips in the expansion: the middle term has a minus in front.
4. Using Cramer's rule when \(|A| = 0\).
